title: Short Stuff: Getting Winded
summary: Short Stuff episode on getting the wind knocked out of you (dyspnea from diaphragm spasm, "frenospasm" as named in the episode). Chuck shares that his daughter Ruby recently had the wind knocked out of her at school and that he once fell from a tree. Josh explains how breathing works via the diaphragm and phrenic nerve, and that the knocked-out-wind reaction is not life threatening and usually resolves within seconds. Josh criticizes online articles claiming the solar plexus is disabled, explaining the solar plexus is a nerve bundle for digestive organs and not responsible for diaphragm control; the hosts cite Kevin Tokoff of Catalyst University's video. They describe first aid: have the person kneel, raise arms overhead, arch back, and breathe deeply and intentionally; if breathing does not normalize within 10 to 15 minutes, go to the hospital because a fractured rib or collapsed lung could be involved. The episode closes with Chuck's tailbone bruise from a golf cart.
topics: getting the wind knocked out of you

segments.title: Opening banter and Ruby's wind knocked out story
segments.summary: Hosts open the short episode. Chuck relates his daughter Ruby getting the wind knocked out of her at school and his own childhood fall from a tree.
topics: getting the wind knocked out of you

segments.title: Listener request and how breathing works
segments.summary: Josh says a listener asked for this topic. He names the condition frenospasm and explains the diaphragm's role in inhaling and exhaling and how air pressure moves air into the lungs.

segments.title: Diaphragm paralysis and spasm from a blow to the chest
segments.summary: Chuck explains breathing is involuntary and that a blow to the chest or solar plexus, or a hard fall onto the back, can spasm or temporarily paralyze the diaphragm. Josh describes the sudden expulsion of air and panic response.

segments.title: Solar plexus myth
segments.summary: Josh says the solar plexus is a nerve bundle for digestive organs and does not control the diaphragm, criticizing articles that repeat the claim. Chuck says the term is shorthand for a target area near the diaphragm.

segments.title: Doctor source on the solar plexus
segments.summary: The hosts credit Kevin Tokoff of Catalyst University with a video explaining that the solar plexus is not the cause and is only in the wrong place at the wrong time.

segments.title: First aid for getting the wind knocked out
segments.summary: Hosts describe the first aid: kneel, raise arms overhead, arch back, breathe deeply and intentionally, stay calm, and use a pillow for support if no one is nearby. Chuck says recovery usually takes seconds to minutes. Josh says if breathing does not return to normal in 10 to 15 minutes, go to the hospital since a fractured rib or collapsed lung could be the cause.
topics: when to go to the hospital

segments.title: Tailbone bruise tangent
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a tailbone bruise from spring break that has lasted weeks, caused by a golf cart incident. Josh suggests an inflatable donut.
